title: On Govt agenda: New Rs 2,800-cr capex scheme for critical minerals
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Infrastructure: energy; Mobilisation of resources · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources across the world and India · GS2 › Effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (China) · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
summary: The Union Cabinet is likely to take up a scheme of about Rs 2,800 crore that offers a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, to build India's domestic critical mineral processing base.
evolution: PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal; storage needs batteries (energy thread).
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: The gap is processing, not only mining: India has little processing capacity and is almost fully import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
GS3 · Industry / GS1 · Resources
India's critical mineral weakness lies in processing; mining ore is of little use without the capacity to refine it.
Concentration as a strategic risk: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions, leaving India open to supply disruptions.
GS2 · India–China / GS3 · Economy
China's hold over mineral processing turns supply chains into tools of pressure, so diversification is national security.
Capex support to start a domestic base: a 30% capital subsidy for four plants (two lithium, two nickel) aims to turn ores into high-purity compounds, with cobalt recovered from nickel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for processing plants target the costliest, riskiest link in India's mineral value chain.
Clean-energy and strategic sectors depend on it: the minerals feed electric mobility, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Energy / Defence industry
Without lithium, nickel and cobalt, India's EV and battery ambitions rest on imported inputs.
Cluster approach: processing parks in four states, each built as an ecosystem for one mineral, backed by a planned stockpile under the National Critical Minerals Mission.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Industrial policy
Mineral-specific parks link resource geography to industry, and a strategic stockpile insures against shocks.
keywords: Mid-stream processing
Refining ores into high-purity chemicals used by battery and electronics makers
GS3 · Industry
India's critical mineral challenge is mid-stream: refining, not just mining.
Weaponisation of supply chains
Using dominance over a resource to pressure other countries
GS2 · IR / GS3 · Economy
China's control of mineral processing shows how supply chains can be weaponised in trade disputes.
Strategic stockpile
A government reserve held to ride out supply disruptions
GS3 · Economy / Security
A critical mineral stockpile works like a strategic oil reserve for the battery age.
Value-chain localisation
Building each stage of production at home
GS3 · Industrial policy
Localising the mineral value chain cuts import dependence from mine to battery.
Resource-based clusters
Industrial parks placed near the raw material they use
GS1 · Location of industries
Odisha's nickel and Gujarat's heavy rare earths show resource-based clustering in practice.
data: Allocation committed for a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme, 2024-25 to 2030-31
National Critical Minerals Mission (Government of India), via IE
The government has committed Rs 500 crore (2024-25 to 2030-31) for a critical mineral stockpile under the NCMM.
examples: Four mineral-specific processing parks
Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh for rare earths, Odisha for nickel, Maharashtra for lithium
GS1 · Distribution of resources · GS3 · Industrial policy
Matching parks to state resources (Odisha's nickel, Gujarat's heavy rare earths) is a model of resource-based industrialisation.
China's leverage over mineral processing
Dominance used as leverage in trade tensions
GS4
GS2 · India–China · GS3 · Economy · GS4 · Ethics in IR
China's use of mineral processing as leverage is a clear example of economic interdependence turned into coercion.
Odisha as a gateway for imported nickel
Eastern location suits imports from Indonesia
GS1 · Location of industries · GS2 · Act East
Odisha's eastern coast lets India process nickel imported from Indonesia, linking resources to the Act East region.
pyqs: The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges for India as the world moves from free trade to protectionism; how to meet them.
Rationale, achievements and improvements of the PLI scheme.
Why India's mining contributes little to GDP despite its Gondwana origin.
Why mining is an environmental hazard; remedial measures.

trend.t: Mineral questions began in physical geography (resource distribution, mining's low GDP share, 2017–2022) and industrial location (2019, 2020). From 2024 the frame shifted to supply chains and geopolitics: India as an alternative to China (2024), protectionism and industrial incentives such as PLI (2025).
trend.watch: Supply-chain resilience and China-plus-one questions are rising since 2024, while mining's environmental cost was asked again in 2025. Critical minerals sit where these meet, so expect a direct question soon.
focus: Industrial policy tools: PLI, capex subsidies, parks
Resource geography and location of processing
Environmental cost of mining and processing

potential: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains. (15 marks)
Why has India remained import-dependent for critical minerals despite its resource base? Examine the role of processing capacity. (10 marks)
How can mineral-specific processing parks promote regional industrial development in India? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains.

answer.t: In November 2026 the Union Cabinet is set to consider a Rs 2,800-crore capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing, as India remains almost fully import-dependent for key critical minerals.

pts.t: Lithium, nickel and cobalt are core to Li-ion batteries for EVs and grid storage.
pts.ex: Needed for India's 500 GW non-fossil goal.

pts.t: Smartphones, semiconductors and electronics depend on these minerals.
Defence systems and speciality steels need rare earths and alloys.
Like oil, control of supply gives power over others.
pts.ex: China's processing dominance used in trade tensions.

pts.t: India relies almost completely on imports for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
Even where ore exists, India lacks refining capacity to make battery-grade compounds.
Global processing is concentrated in China, which has curbed exports of some minerals in the past.
pts.ex: Export curbs on gallium and germanium (2023).

pts.t: Large parts of India's mineral potential remain unexplored.
Processing plants are costly and technology-intensive, deterring private investment.
Mining and chemical processing can damage land, water and local communities.
30% capital subsidy for lithium and nickel plants under the proposed scheme.
A mission-mode approach to exploration, processing and overseas assets, with a planned stockpile.
pts.ex: Rs 500 crore committed for stockpiling (2024-25 to 2030-31).

pts.t: Ecosystems in four states matched to their resources.
pts.ex: Odisha for nickel, Gujarat and AP for rare earths.

pts.t: Secure supplies abroad through state firms and partners.
pts.ex: KABIL; India's membership of the Minerals Security Partnership.

pts.t: Recover minerals from used batteries and e-waste to reduce fresh demand.
Strict environmental norms and benefit-sharing with mining communities.

answer.t: Just as oil security shaped the last century, building domestic processing, diverse partners and a strategic stockpile will decide India's energy and strategic autonomy in this one.

title: An alliance for multilateralism by other means
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora: their structure and mandate; Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations; Environmental ethics
summary: The Partners for Multilateralism (P4M), launched at the 81st UNGA week and co-sponsored by India among others, commits to strengthening multilateral cooperation; the author argues it needs a concrete plan, clear principles and public engagement to succeed.
evolution: BRICS Parliamentary Forum seeks UNSC reform.
P4M, co-sponsored by India, pledges to strengthen multilateral cooperation.
ideas: Multilateralism under severe pressure: the US, a principal founder and long-time guarantor of the system, is rejecting it in word and deed, and other major players flout rules with impunity.
GS2 · International institutions
With the system's own guarantor walking away, middle and smaller powers must carry multilateralism.
A bridge across divides: co-sponsored by Australia, Brazil, Barbados, Canada, the EU, India and Kenya and signed by 18 more, P4M joins large and small countries of the Global South and North.
GS2 · Groupings involving India
P4M's mixed membership makes it a rare bridge between the Global North and South.

Reform language reflects a power shift: its pledge of cooperation that is 'open, fair, equitable, inclusive' echoes the South's long demand, now heard in a North weakened by Western turmoil and Transatlantic strain.
GS2 · Global order / Global South
The North's new receptiveness to reform reflects the Global South's growing clout and the West's own turmoil.
Plan and principles, or failure: P4M needs an action plan with costs and how they are shared, and clear principles that set it apart from efforts such as China's four Global Initiatives.
GS2 · Effect of policies of other countries
Coalitions without costed plans and clear principles join the list of well-intended but failed initiatives.
Engage people and the planet: reform drives fail when they ignore affected populations; P4M's diversity could offer ideas on deep ecology and interspecies coexistence for a new framework.
GS2 · Global governance / GS4 · Environmental ethics
Multilateralism will regain legitimacy only when it engages the public and protects the planet, not just states.
keywords: Minilateralism / coalition of the willing
Small, flexible groups of like-minded states acting where universal bodies stall
GS2 · Groupings
When universal institutions stall, coalitions of the willing like P4M keep cooperation alive.
Rules-based order
An international system governed by agreed norms rather than power
GS2 · International order
P4M's commitment to institutions and rule of law defends the rules-based order.
Reformed multilateralism
India's call to update global institutions to reflect today's realities
GS2 · India's foreign policy
India's co-sponsorship of P4M fits its long call for reformed multilateralism.
Bridging power
A country able to connect rival blocs
GS2 · India's global role
India's presence in P4M, BRICS and the Quad shows its role as a bridging power.
Deep ecology
A view that nature has value in itself, not only for human use
GS4 · Environmental ethics
Deep ecology asks global institutions to protect the planet for its own sake.
examples: Partners for Multilateralism (P4M)
Launched at the 81st UNGA week, co-sponsored by India
GS2 · International institutions · groupings · Essay
P4M shows middle powers trying to save multilateralism as the great powers turn away from it.
US rejection of the system it built
A founder and guarantor turning away
GS2 · Global order · Essay
The US turning against institutions it founded shows that even the architects of an order can abandon it.
China's four Global Initiatives
Rival visions of global governance
GS2 · India–China · global order
China's Global Initiatives show the contest over who will write the next rules of global governance.
pyqs: Unresolved UN reform amid East–West imbalance and the US vs Russo-Chinese entanglement.
BRICS as a counterweight in global governance amplifying the Global South.
Challenges as the world moves from free trade and multilateralism to protectionism and bilateralism.
Key areas of WTO reform amid trade war, keeping India's interests in mind.
Has India's image as leader of the marginalised nations faded in the new global order?
Waning globalisation and the rise of sovereign nationalism.

trend.t: Questions moved from the mandates of specific bodies (WTO, Bretton Woods, UNESCO, 2013–2019) to the crisis of the system itself: WTO reform amid trade war (2018), unresolved UN reform and great-power rivalry (2025), the retreat from multilateralism (2025) and BRICS as a voice of the Global South (2026).
trend.watch: Since 2025 UPSC asks about the crisis of multilateralism almost every year. Prepare why the order is weakening, who is reshaping it and India's role as a bridge for the Global South.
focus: Crisis of multilateralism and great-power retreat
Reform of the UN, WTO and other institutions

potential: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role. (15 marks)
What are the limits of coalitions of the willing in reforming global governance? (10 marks)
"In international relations, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must." How can a rules-based order change this? (10 marks, GS4)

practice.q: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role.

answer.t: In September 2026, India, the EU, Brazil, Canada, Kenya, Australia and Barbados co-sponsored the Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) at the 81st UNGA, just as the US, the system's founder, turns away from it.

pts.t: The US rejects institutions it built, in word and deed.
pts.ex: Withdrawals from the WHO and the Paris Agreement.

pts.t: Rules are flouted with frequency and impunity.
pts.ex: Wars in Europe and West Asia.

pts.t: Key bodies cannot act or reform.
pts.ex: WTO Appellate Body non-functional since 2019; UNSC reform stalled.

pts.t: Institutions reflect 1945, not today's balance of power.
Competing models of global governance divide states.
Institutions seem distant from the people they affect.
Mixed membership builds trust across old divides.
pts.ex: P4M joins large and small states of both.

pts.t: Commitment to cooperation that is open, fair, equitable and inclusive.
Small coalitions act faster than universal bodies.
Groupings amplify developing countries' demands.
pts.ex: BRICS; India's Voice of the Global South summits.

pts.t: Declarations without costed plans fade.
Without clarity, they overlap with rival initiatives.
Ignoring affected people breeds discontent.
Many small coalitions can weaken universal institutions.
India sits in the Quad, BRICS, SCO and P4M and can link rival blocs.
Push the South's agenda on finance, climate and technology.
pts.ex: African Union's G20 membership under India's 2023 presidency.

pts.t: Press for UNSC and WTO reform with like-minded partners.
Back P4M with concrete projects, costs and burden-sharing.
Bring civilisational ideas such as Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and LiFE into global norms.
pts.ex: G20 theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'.

pts.t: Keep commitments, as on climate targets met early.

answer.t: As great powers retreat, coalitions like P4M can keep multilateralism alive; India, as a bridging power, can help turn declarations into a fairer, workable order.

title: NSA Doval, Vietnamese ministers hold bilateral talks to boost security
syllabus: GS2 › Bilateral relations; Act East; Indo-Pacific · GS3 › Security cooperation
summary: Minor topic: NSA Ajit Doval held talks in Hanoi with Vietnam's defence, public security and foreign ministers to strengthen 'multifaceted' ties.
ideas: Security at the core of Act East: Doval met Vietnam's Defence Minister, Public Security Minister and Foreign Minister; both sides reviewed defence cooperation and agreed to strengthen it.
GS2 · India–Vietnam / Act East
Security and defence cooperation with Vietnam anchors India's Act East policy.
A partner in the Indo-Pacific: Vietnam, a key ASEAN state on the South China Sea, is central to India's maritime and regional strategy.
GS2 · Indo-Pacific
Close ties with Vietnam strengthen India's position in a contested South China Sea.
keywords: Act East Policy
India's strategic engagement with South-East Asia
GS2 · Foreign policy
Defence ties with Vietnam give substance to the Act East Policy.
examples: NSA Doval in Hanoi
Talks with Vietnam's defence, security and foreign ministers
GS2 · Act East, Indo-Pacific · GS3 · Security cooperation
Doval's Hanoi visit shows India deepening security partnerships in South-East Asia.
pyqs: Maritime security and freedom of navigation in the South China Sea.
Geopolitical significance of the South China Sea.
